concept.shortExplanation: The perceptron is the smallest thing that can honestly be called a trained model: a weight per input, a bias, and a rule that fires if the weighted sum clears zero. Training is one line — when it gets an example wrong, nudge the weights toward that example. Run that nudge over a dataset and a decision boundary emerges without anyone designing it. The perceptron you are about to train is real, initialised randomly, and updated in the browser one example at a time.
concept.ahaMoment: You never told it where the line goes. You only told it, repeatedly, when it was wrong — and the line assembled itself out of those corrections. Every model in this course is that same loop with more parameters.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The in-browser trainer failed to start. Reload the chapter to retry — no download is involved, this model is trained locally from scratch.

levels.title: Step Through Training
levels.instructions: Press step to feed one example at a time. Watch the weight vector rotate whenever the perceptron is wrong, and stop when the boundary separates both classes.
hints: Watch the weight vector — the line only rotates when the perceptron misclassifies the sample currently under the cursor ring. Step through and see which samples trigger a move.
These starting weights already point close to a working boundary, so accuracy begins right at the pass line before you've done anything. It shouldn't take many updates once you start stepping.
Just keep pressing Step (or use ×10) — from these starting weights, a single weight update is enough to reach 100% accuracy.

levels.title: Converge Fast
levels.instructions: Same rule, harder data. Tune the learning rate and reach full separation in as few updates as possible — the score is the number of weight updates you needed.
hints: The learning rate scales how far each correction moves the boundary — but this run starts at exactly zero weights. Think about what that means for the very first few updates.

When weights start at zero, the sign of every 'is this point right or wrong' test scales uniformly with the learning rate — which means the sequence of right/wrong decisions the perceptron makes turns out to be exactly the same no matter what η you pick, as long as it's positive.
Set the learning rate to anything reasonable and just run — from a zero start, this dataset converges in exactly 41 updates regardless of η, comfortably inside the 80-update mark for three stars.

levels.title: The XOR Wall
levels.instructions: Now try XOR. Train as long as you like — you cannot beat this, and finding out exactly how well you can do is the point. Get as close to the ceiling as a single linear boundary allows.
hints: No amount of stepping through training will separate XOR with a single straight line — that's the whole point of this level. You have to place the boundary by hand with the weight sliders.

A single line can't cleanly split XOR's four quadrants, but it can sacrifice one quadrant and get the other three right — that's the best any straight boundary can do here. Try angling the line diagonally rather than along an axis.

Set w0 ≈ 0.12, w1 ≈ −0.10, bias ≈ 0.08 (any scaled version of that same direction and ratio works too, e.g. w0=0.96, w1=−0.80, bias=0.64) — that reaches about 0.77 accuracy, comfortably past three stars.
